newsitem.title: UK: SB sees deadlock on EU parallel drug imports.
newsitem.headline: SB sees deadlock on EU parallel drug imports.

text.p: The chief executive of SmithKline Beecham Plc (SB), Jan Leschly, said on Tuesday that large European research-based drug manufacturers remained unhappy with EU regulations for so-called "parallel import" drugs and continued to press the Commission for a change in policy.
"Quite honestly, we don't have the solution just now," Leschy told a news conference in London to review his company's financial performance in 1996.
He said that SB continued to discuss the best ways to open the pharmaceuticals market to full competition with Martin Bangemann, the European Commissioner for Industry.
"We are still lobbying the Commission... (Parallel imports) can have an impact on our business in the long run and we certainly hope (the rules) can be changed over time," he said.
Last December the European Court of Justice made two rulings that effectively said parallel importing was permitted under EU single market legislation.
This means intermediary firms can buy branded but unpatented drugs from countries like Spain and Portugal where they are cheaper.
They can then sell them in other markets where branded prices are higher because patents are enforced or manufacturers' prices are controlled.
Leschly said that allowing parallel imports made no sense while price controls on drugs remain in many EU states.
"It is not reasonable that you have parallel imports when you have price controls," he told reporters.
SmithKline's top priority was to achieve free market pricing in Europe so that the retailing playing field can be levelled, he added.

The SB chief described Britain's PPRS scheme, which links the profit margin allowed on branded medicines sold to the National Health Service, as the "least worst" control method and said his firm preferred it to other mechanisms used in Europe.
